tip: 랑 (rang) = with/and, casual: 동료랑 (dongnyorang = with a colleague).
할 일 (hallil) is literally 'will-do work': 할 (hal) turns 하다 (hada = do) into a label for the noun after it. Korean builds 'things to do' straight from the verb.
다녀요 (danyeoyo), from 다니다 (danida = go regularly), is a common way to say you work somewhere: 은행에 다녀요 (eunhaeng-e danyeoyo) – showing up routinely is the job.
스트레스를 받아요 (seuteureseureul badayo) = 'receive stress' = to be stressed.
실 (sil) is a 'room' ending: 회의실 (hoeisil) = meeting room, 화장실 (hwajangsil) = bathroom. Spot 실 and it's usually some kind of room.
후에 (hue = after) comes after its noun: 회의 후에 (hoei hue) is literally 'meeting-after'. Korean time words normally trail the thing they anchor to – reversed from English.
제가 사요 (jega sayo), 'I'm buying', is the usual way to offer to treat – 사다 (sada = buy) normally covers picking up the bill.
에 (e) can link food pairings: 치킨에 맥주 (chikin-e maekju) = chicken with beer. The combo is so beloved it compressed into one word, 치맥 (chimaek).
번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 세 번 (se beon = three times).
많아서 (manaseo) packs 'because there's a lot' into one word – the -아서 (-aseo) ending fuses the cause onto the verb, so no separate 'because' appears.
별로 (byeollo) with a negative verb = not really: 별로 없어요 (byeollo eopseoyo) = not much.
월급날 (wolgeumnal = payday) has a sound trap: it's spelled with ㅂ (b) before ㄴ (n), but ㅂ turns into ㅁ (m) there – say -mn-, never -pn-.
-고 (go) links actions in order: 샤워하고 (syawohago = shower and then).
못 먹었어요 (mon meogeosseoyo) = couldn't eat: 못 (mot) means circumstances stopped you. 안 (an) would mean you chose to skip breakfast.
수고했어요 (sugohaesseoyo) = 'you worked hard', a common end-of-day goodbye at work.
저 먼저 가요 (jeo meonjeo gayo) is the polite 'I'm leaving first' you say on the way out of the office.
휴가를 (hyugareul) pairs with 쓰다 (sseuda), which covers both 'write' and 'use' – here it shows up as 쓸 거예요 (sseul kkeoyeyo = will use).
Most city Koreans live in 아파트 (apateu), big high-rise complexes.
층 (cheung) = floor, with Sino numbers: 십오 층 (sibo cheung = 15th floor).
개 (gae) is the all-purpose counting word, used with native numbers: 두 개 (du gae = two things).
마다 (mada) sticks straight onto a noun: 주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend. Nothing else is needed – 마다 carries 'every' on its own.
Korean often uses 'spin' for running a machine: 청소기를 돌려요 (cheongsogireul dollyeoyo = run the vacuum).
Korean picks the wash verb by what you wash – 빨다 (ppalda) is the one for fabric: 이불을 빨았어요 (ibureul pparasseoyo). Dishes and your body take different verbs.
물을 줬어요 (mureul jwosseoyo) = 'gave water' = watered the plants.
-기 전에 (gi jeone) = before doing: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone = before sleeping).
분리수거 (bullisugeo) = mandatory trash sorting, an apartment-life ritual.
깜빡했어요 (kkamppakaesseoyo) = 'it slipped my mind', the casual spoken way to say you forgot to do something.
-비 (bi) = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi) = delivery fee.
놓아 주세요 (noa juseyo) ends with 주세요, the polite form of 주다 (juda = give) – tacking it onto a verb asks for the action as a favor for you.
-고 싶어요 (go sipeoyo) = want to: 먹고 싶어요 (meokko sipeoyo) = want to eat.
